title: How Bones Grow and Heal
summary: How bones grow through childhood, what calcium and vitamin D do for them, and how the body heals a broken bone step by step.
poll: Bones stop changing once you become an adult.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
You have a skeleton inside you. It is made of bones.

Bones hold you up. Bones keep soft parts safe too. They are like a shield.

Babies have more bones than grown-ups. Some bones join as you grow. A grown-up has 206 bones.

Bones can grow. Near the end of a bone is a soft spot. It helps the bone get longer. This is fast when you are young.

Bones need calcium. Calcium is in milk. It makes bones hard. It makes bones strong.

A bone can break. Your body can heal it! Blood makes a clot first. Soft new tissue grows next. Then it turns hard again.

Take care of your bones. Drink milk. Eat good food. Play each day. Your bones will grow strong.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
You have a skeleton inside your body. It is made of many bones joined together.

Bones hold your body up. They also keep soft parts safe. They work like a shield for your heart.

Babies have more bones than grown-ups. Some small bones join as you grow. A grown-up has 206 bones.

Bones can grow longer too. Near the end of a long bone is a soft spot. It helps the bone get longer. This growing is fastest when you are a kid.

Bones need a mineral called calcium to stay strong. Calcium is in milk, cheese, and some plants. It makes your bones hard and strong.

A bone can crack or break. This is a fracture. Luckily, your body can heal it! First, blood makes a clot at the break. Then soft new tissue grows there. After some weeks, it turns into hard bone again.

Take good care of your bones. Drink milk, eat good food, and play outside each day. This will help your bones grow strong for life.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
You have a skeleton inside your body, made of many bones joined together. Without it, your body would be too soft to stand up.

Bones do several jobs. They hold your body up so you can stand and walk. They also keep soft parts safe, like a shield around your heart and lungs.

Babies have more bones than grown-ups do. Many small bones join together as a child grows. By the time you are an adult, you have 206 bones.

Bones also grow longer as you grow. Near the end of a long bone is a soft spot made of special stuff. It helps the bone stretch and grow longer. This happens fastest when you are a kid or a teen.

Bones need a mineral called calcium to stay strong. Calcium is found in milk, cheese, and some green plants. It is calcium that makes bones hard enough to hold your weight.

Sometimes a bone cracks or breaks. Doctors call this a fracture. Luckily, your body can heal a broken bone! First, blood collects and forms a clot at the break. Then the body builds new, soft tissue there. After some weeks, that tissue slowly turns into hard bone again.

Taking care of your bones now matters for your whole life. Drinking milk, eating good food, and staying active outside all help your bones grow as strong as they can.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
You have a skeleton inside your body, made of many bones joined together. Without it, your body would be too soft to stand up straight.

Bones do several jobs. They hold your body up so you can stand, sit, and walk. They also protect your soft organs, almost like a shield around your heart and lungs.

Babies are born with more bones than grown-ups have. Many small bones join together as a child grows older. By the time a person is an adult, the body usually has 206 bones.

Bones also grow longer as a child grows. Near the end of a long bone, like a leg bone, there is a soft spot made of special stuff. This soft spot lets the bone stretch and grow longer. This growing happens fastest during childhood, then it slows down.

To stay strong, bones need a mineral called calcium. Calcium is in foods like milk, cheese, and leafy green plants. It is calcium that makes bones hard enough to hold your weight. Your body also needs vitamin D to take in calcium. Sunlight helps your skin make some of this vitamin.

Sometimes a bone cracks or breaks. Doctors call this a fracture. Luckily, the body can heal a broken bone on its own. First, blood collects at the break and forms a clot. Next, the body builds new, soft tissue there. After some weeks, that tissue slowly hardens into solid bone again.

Taking care of your bones now matters for your whole life. Drinking milk, eating healthy food, getting some sun, and staying active all help your bones grow strong.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
Your body has a skeleton made of many bones joined together. Without it, your body could not stand up straight.

The skeleton does several jobs. It holds your body up so you can stand, sit, and walk. It also protects your soft organs, almost like a shield around your heart and lungs.

Babies are born with more bones than adults have. Many small bones join together as a child grows older. By adulthood, the body usually has 206 bones.

Bones also grow longer as a child grows. Near the end of a long bone, like a bone in the leg, is a soft spot made of a flexible material. This soft spot lets the bone stretch and grow longer. This growing happens fastest during childhood, then it slows down and stops.

Bone is not solid all the way through. A hard outer layer gives bone its strength, while a softer, spongy layer sits underneath. Inside many bones is marrow, a soft tissue that makes the blood cells your body needs.

Bones depend on nutrients to stay strong, especially a mineral called calcium. Calcium is in foods like milk, cheese, and leafy greens. Vitamin D is another key nutrient, since it helps your body take in calcium from food, and sunlight lets your skin make some of this vitamin.

Sometimes a bone cracks or breaks, which doctors call a fracture. Luckily, the body knows how to repair a broken bone on its own. First, blood collects at the break and forms a clot. Next, the body builds soft new tissue there. After some weeks, that tissue hardens into solid bone again.

Taking care of your skeleton matters for your whole life. Eating healthy food, drinking milk, getting some sun, and staying active all help your bones grow and repair themselves.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
The human body has a skeleton made of many bones joined together. Without it, the body could not stand upright at all.

The skeleton performs several jobs. It supports the body so a person can stand, sit, and walk, and it also protects delicate organs, almost like a shield around the heart and lungs.

Infants are born with more bones than adults have. Many small bones gradually join together as a child grows older. By adulthood, the body typically contains 206 bones.

Bones also grow longer as a child develops. Near the end of a long bone, such as one in the arm or leg, there is a soft region made of flexible material. This region allows the bone to stretch and grow longer. This growth happens fastest during childhood, then slows and eventually stops.

Bone tissue is not solid all the way through. A hard outer layer gives bone much of its strength, while a softer, spongy layer lies underneath. Inside many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that produces the blood cells the body needs.

Bones rely on certain nutrients to remain strong, especially a mineral called calcium. Calcium occurs in foods such as milk, cheese, and leafy greens. Vitamin D is another important nutrient, since it helps the body absorb calcium from food, and sunlight allows the skin to produce some of this vitamin.

Occasionally a bone cracks or breaks, an injury doctors classify as a fracture. Fortunately, the body has a remarkable ability to repair a broken bone on its own. First, blood collects at the injury and forms a clot. Next, the body constructs new, soft tissue around the broken ends. After several weeks, this tissue gradually hardens into solid, working bone.

Caring for your skeleton during childhood matters for your entire life. Eating nutritious food, drinking milk, getting adequate sunlight, and staying active all help bones grow and repair themselves well.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
The human skeleton, made of many individual bones joined together, provides support that allows the body to stand upright, protects organs such as the heart and lungs, and gives muscles a place to pull so the body can move.

Infants are born with considerably more bony and cartilage pieces than adults ultimately keep, because many small pieces gradually fuse together during childhood and adolescence as skeletal growth proceeds. By early adulthood, the skeleton typically consists of exactly 206 bones.

Bones also grow longer throughout childhood and adolescence. This growth occurs at growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those in the arms and legs. Cartilage cells within these plates gradually multiply and convert into solid bone, a process called ossification. Once puberty concludes, the growth plates close permanently, and the bone can no longer lengthen.

Bone tissue is not solid all the way through. A hard, dense outer layer provides much of its strength, while a lighter, more porous layer of spongy bone lies beneath it. At the core of many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that produces the red and white blood cells the body needs.

Bone strength depends heavily on minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, which become deposited within a flexible framework inside the bone. Because the body cannot produce calcium on its own, this mineral must come from foods such as dairy products and leafy greens. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium from food, and sunlight allows the skin to produce some of this vitamin.

When a fracture occurs, a well-coordinated healing process begins almost immediately. Blood clots at the break within hours, and over the following weeks, cells gradually convert the clot into new bone. During a remodeling stage that can continue for months, excess or oddly shaped bone is removed while precisely shaped new bone is deposited, allowing the fracture site to regenerate a shape nearly like the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also influences bone strength throughout life. When bones bear weight during running or climbing, cells add more mineral content and bone density increases, while long periods without activity can reduce it.

versions.text:
The human skeleton, composed of numerous individual bones joined together, provides mechanical support that allows the body to maintain an upright posture, protects delicate organs such as the heart and lungs, and gives muscles rigid attachment points so the body can generate movement.

By early adulthood, the skeleton typically consists of exactly 206 distinct bones.

Bones also increase in length throughout childhood and adolescence. This lengthening occurs at growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those in the arms and legs. Cartilage cells within these plates gradually multiply and progressively convert into solid bone, a process known as ossification. Once puberty concludes, these growth plates close permanently, and the bone can no longer lengthen at all.

Bone tissue is nevertheless far from solid all the way through. A hard, dense outer layer provides much of its overall strength, while a lighter, more porous layer of spongy bone lies beneath it. At the core of many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that continuously produces the red and white blood cells the body needs.

Bone strength depends heavily upon minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, which become deposited within a flexible framework inside the bone. Because the body cannot synthesize calcium on its own, this essential mineral must come from foods such as dairy products and leafy greens. Vitamin D substantially helps the body absorb calcium from food, and sunlight additionally allows the skin to produce some of this vitamin.

When a fracture occurs, a remarkably coordinated healing process begins almost immediately. Blood clots at the break within hours, and over the following weeks, specialized cells gradually convert the clot into new bone. During a prolonged remodeling stage that can continue for several months, excess or oddly shaped bone is systematically removed while precisely shaped new bone is simultaneously deposited, allowing the fracture site to regenerate a shape nearly indistinguishable from the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also substantially influences bone strength throughout an individual's life. When bones repeatedly bear weight during running, jumping, or climbing, specialized cells add more mineral content and bone density gradually increases, whereas long periods without activity tend to reduce it.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
The human skeleton, composed of numerous individual bones joined together, provides mechanical support that allows the body to maintain an upright posture, protects delicate organs such as the heart and lungs, and gives muscles rigid attachment points that enable the body to generate coordinated movement.

Infants are born with considerably more bony and cartilaginous pieces than adults ultimately retain, because many small pieces gradually fuse together during childhood and adolescence as skeletal development steadily proceeds. By early adulthood, the skeleton typically consists of exactly 206 distinct bones, even though it began with far more individual components.

Bones also increase steadily in length throughout childhood and adolescence. This lengthening occurs at specialized regions called growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those in the arms and legs. Cartilage cells within these plates gradually multiply and progressively convert into solid bone, a process known as ossification that intensifies during adolescent growth spurts. Once puberty concludes, these growth plates close permanently, and the bone can no longer lengthen at all.

Bone tissue is nevertheless far from solid throughout its structure. A hard, dense outer layer provides much of its overall strength, while a lighter, more porous layer of spongy bone lies beneath it. At the core of many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that continuously manufactures the red and white blood cells circulating throughout the body.

Bone strength depends heavily upon minerals, particularly calcium and phosphorus, which become deposited within a flexible protein framework inside the bone. Because the body cannot synthesize calcium independently, this essential mineral must come from nutrient-rich foods such as dairy products and leafy greens. Vitamin D substantially improves the body's ability to absorb calcium from food, and sunlight additionally allows the skin to manufacture some of this vital vitamin.

When a fracture occurs, a remarkably coordinated healing process begins almost immediately. Blood escaping from damaged vessels clots around the broken ends within hours, and over the following weeks, specialized cells gradually convert this clot into new bone. During a prolonged remodeling phase that can continue for several months, excess or misshapen bone is systematically removed by cells called osteoclasts while precisely shaped new bone is deposited by cells called osteoblasts, allowing the fracture site to regenerate a structure nearly indistinguishable from the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also substantially influences bone strength throughout an individual's life. When bones repeatedly bear weight during activities such as running, jumping, or climbing, specialized cells detect this loading and add more mineral content, gradually increasing bone density, whereas prolonged inactivity tends to reduce it considerably.

versions.text:
The human skeleton, composed of numerous individual bones joined together, provides mechanical support that allows the body to maintain an upright posture, protects delicate internal organs such as the heart and lungs, and furnishes muscles with rigid attachment points that enable the body to generate coordinated, purposeful movement.

Infants are born with considerably more bony and cartilaginous elements than adults ultimately retain, because numerous small pieces gradually fuse together throughout childhood and adolescence as skeletal development steadily proceeds. This lengthening occurs at specialized regions called growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those in the arms and legs. Cartilage cells within these plates gradually multiply and progressively convert into solid bone, a process known as ossification that intensifies markedly during adolescent growth spurts. Bone tissue is nevertheless far from uniformly solid throughout its structure. Blood escaping from damaged vessels clots around the broken ends within hours, and over the following weeks, specialized cells gradually convert this clot into new bone. During a prolonged remodeling phase that can continue for several months, excess or misshapen bone is systematically removed by cells called osteoclasts while precisely shaped new bone is simultaneously deposited by cells called osteoblasts, ultimately allowing the fracture site to regenerate a structure nearly indistinguishable from the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also substantially influences bone strength throughout an individual's life. versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
The human skeleton, an intricate internal framework composed of numerous individual bones joined together, performs several essential and interconnected functions: it provides mechanical support that allows the body to maintain an upright posture, it protects delicate internal organs such as the heart, lungs, and brain, and it provides rigid attachment points that enable muscles to generate coordinated movement, thereby making complex physical activity possible and, in doing so, granting the body its distinctive capacity for locomotion.

Remarkably, an infant is born possessing considerably more bony and cartilaginous elements than an adult ultimately retains, because numerous small pieces gradually fuse together throughout childhood and adolescence as skeletal development steadily proceeds. By the time this process concludes in early adulthood, the skeleton typically consists of exactly 206 distinct bones, even though it began with far more individual components.

Bones also increase steadily in length throughout childhood and adolescence. This lengthening occurs at specialized regions called growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those found in the arms and legs. Cartilage cells within these plates gradually multiply and progressively convert into solid bone, a process known as ossification that intensifies markedly during adolescent growth spurts and is orchestrated by precise genetic and hormonal signals, allowing the bones to lengthen in a controlled, orderly manner. Once puberty concludes, these growth plates close permanently, and further increases in bone length become biologically impossible.

Bone tissue is nevertheless far from uniformly solid throughout its structure. A dense, compact outer layer provides considerable strength, while a lighter, more porous layer of spongy bone lies beneath it, substantially reducing overall weight without sacrificing structural integrity. At the core of many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that continuously manufactures the red and white blood cells circulating throughout the entire body.

Bone strength depends heavily upon minerals, particularly calcium and phosphorus, which become deposited within a flexible protein framework to give bone its characteristic rigidity and resistance to breaking. Because the body cannot synthesize calcium independently, this essential mineral must be obtained through nutrient-rich foods such as dairy products and leafy green vegetables. Vitamin D, meanwhile, substantially improves the intestine's capacity to absorb calcium from digested food, and sunlight exposure additionally allows the skin to manufacture a portion of this vital vitamin, a deficiency that, left unaddressed, can compromise bone integrity later in life.

When a fracture occurs, a remarkably coordinated healing process begins almost immediately. Within hours, blood escaping from damaged vessels clots around the broken ends, forming a protective hematoma. Over the following weeks, specialized cells gradually convert this clot into new bone, and during a prolonged remodeling phase that can continue for several months, excess or misshapen bone is systematically removed by cells called osteoclasts while precisely shaped new bone is simultaneously deposited by cells called osteoblasts, a cellular partnership that persists, at a slower pace, throughout adult life as well, ultimately allowing the fracture site to regenerate a structure nearly indistinguishable from the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also substantially influences bone strength throughout an individual's life. When bones repeatedly bear weight during activities such as running, jumping, or climbing, specialized cells detect this mechanical loading and respond by depositing additional mineral content, gradually increasing overall bone density, whereas prolonged inactivity tends to reduce it considerably.

Because peak bone density achieved by early adulthood strongly influences skeletal health many decades later, consuming calcium-rich food, obtaining adequate sunlight, and engaging in regular weight-bearing physical activity during these formative years represents one of the more genuinely valuable long-term investments a young person can make, one whose benefits persist well into later adulthood, underscoring the lifelong, cumulative nature of skeletal health.

versions.title: How Bones Grow and Heal
versions.text:
The skeleton, the intricate framework of bones that forms the body's internal structure, performs several indispensable functions simultaneously: it provides mechanical support that allows the body to maintain an upright posture, it furnishes rigid attachment points that enable muscles to generate movement, and it forms a protective enclosure that shields delicate internal organs, including the heart, lungs, and brain, from everyday impacts.

Remarkably, an infant is born with approximately 300 individual bony and cartilaginous elements, considerably more than an adult possesses, because numerous separate pieces gradually fuse together throughout childhood and adolescence. By the time skeletal development concludes in early adulthood, these fusions have reduced the total to the familiar count of 206 distinct bones.

Longitudinal bone growth occurs at specialized regions called growth plates, bands of cartilage located near the ends of long bones such as those in the arms and legs. Throughout childhood and particularly during adolescent growth spurts, cartilage cells within these plates multiply and gradually convert into solid bone, a process called ossification, causing the bones to lengthen steadily. Once puberty concludes, these growth plates close permanently, and further increases in height through bone lengthening become impossible.

Internally, bone is far from a simple, solid substance. A dense, compact outer layer provides strength, while a lighter, honeycombed layer of spongy bone lies beneath it, reducing weight without sacrificing structural integrity. At the core of many bones lies marrow, a soft tissue that manufactures the red and white blood cells circulating throughout the body.

Bone tissue depends heavily on minerals, particularly calcium and phosphorus, which are deposited within a flexible protein framework to give bone its characteristic rigidity and resistance to fracture. Because the body cannot synthesize calcium independently, this essential mineral must be obtained through nutrient-rich foods such as dairy products, leafy green vegetables, and fortified cereals. Vitamin D, meanwhile, dramatically improves the intestine's ability to absorb calcium from digested food, and sunlight exposure allows the skin to manufacture a portion of this vital vitamin.

When a fracture occurs, a remarkably orchestrated healing sequence immediately begins. Within hours, blood escaping from damaged vessels clots around the broken ends, forming a protective hematoma. Over the following one to two weeks, this clot is gradually replaced by a soft, cartilage-like structure called a soft callus, which bridges the fracture site and provides preliminary stability. Specialized cells then convert this soft callus into a hard callus of genuine bone over several additional weeks, and finally, during a prolonged remodeling phase that can continue for months, cells called osteoclasts dissolve excess or misshapen bone while cells called osteoblasts deposit new, precisely shaped bone, ultimately allowing the fracture site to regenerate a structure nearly indistinguishable from the bone's original form.

Mechanical stress also influences bone strength throughout life. When bones repeatedly bear weight during activities such as running, jumping, or climbing, specialized cells detect this mechanical loading and respond by depositing additional mineral content, gradually increasing bone density. Conversely, bones that remain largely unloaded, whether through prolonged inactivity or extended time in microgravity, tend to lose density over time.

Because the skeleton continues developing throughout childhood and adolescence, and because peak bone density achieved by early adulthood strongly influences skeletal health decades later, consuming calcium-rich and vitamin D-rich foods, obtaining adequate sunlight, and engaging in regular weight-bearing physical activity during these formative years represents one of the most consequential long-term investments a young person can make in their own future health.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does marrow do inside a bone?
options: It makes the outer layer of bone harder and thicker.
It produces the body's red and white blood cells.
It turns into calcium over time, as a child grows.
It closes a bone's growth plate in old age.
questions.why: The article says marrow is a soft tissue that produces the blood cells your body needs.

wrong.A: The hard outer layer is a separate part of the bone.
wrong.C: Marrow does not turn into calcium.
wrong.D: Growth plates close due to puberty, not marrow.

questions.stem: What is a joint, according to the article?
options: A thin strand inside a muscle fiber.
A kind of food that helps muscles grow strong.
A place where two bones meet and can move.
A cord that connects muscle to bone.
questions.why: The article discusses bones meeting at movable points as part of how the skeleton functions.

wrong.A: A strand inside a muscle is not a joint.
wrong.D: A cord connecting muscle to bone is a tendon, not a joint.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word tissue mean?
options: A type of exercise for muscles and joints in the body.
A group of similar cells working together in the body.
A kind of bone found in joints, such as the knee and hip.
A tool doctors use to check injuries in the clinic.
questions.why: The article uses tissue to describe marrow and the soft material that forms during healing.

wrong.C: Tissue is not a kind of bone.
wrong.D: Tissue is not a tool.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the information about healing after the paragraph on nutrients?
options: By comparing human bones to animal bones
By listing bones from smallest to largest
By describing the repair steps in the order they happen
By telling a story about one doctor's whole career
questions.why: The article describes a clot forming, then soft tissue, then hard bone, in the order these steps occur.

wrong.B: The article does not rank bones by size.
wrong.D: There is no story about a doctor.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a child not getting enough calcium or vitamin D?
options: The child's bones may not grow as strong as they could.
The child's marrow will stop making blood cells.
The child's skeleton will have more than 206 bones.
The child's bones will fracture into dust.
questions.why: Since calcium and vitamin D help make bones hard and strong, not getting enough can leave bones weaker.

wrong.B: The article does not link marrow function to calcium.
wrong.C: Bone count is linked to fusing as a child grows, not nutrients.
wrong.D: The article never describes bones turning to dust.

questions.stem: Khalid broke his arm and the doctor put it in a cast for six weeks. Based on the article, why might the doctor wait that long?
options: Because marrow needs six weeks to protect the brain.
Because calcium takes six weeks to reach the stomach.
Because new bone tissue needs time to repair the break.
Because growth plates close after six weeks.
questions.why: The article explains that healing new tissue into solid bone again takes several weeks.

wrong.A: Marrow does not protect the brain.
wrong.B: The article does not give a six-week timeline for digestion.
wrong.D: Growth plates close near the end of the teenage years, not in six weeks.

questions.stem: What can you infer about a bone's outer layer and its spongy inner layer?
options: They work together to make bones both strong and lighter.
They are exactly the same kind of tissue.
Only the spongy layer protects organs.
The outer layer contains all of the body's marrow.
questions.why: The hard outer layer gives strength while the spongy layer reduces weight, so together they balance strength and lightness.

wrong.B: The article describes them as different.
wrong.C: Protection comes from the skeleton as a whole.
wrong.D: Marrow is at the core of bones, not in the outer layer.

MID.prompt: Write advice for a younger student about how to keep their skeleton healthy. Use at least three ideas from the article and explain why each one helps.
checklist: I gave at least three pieces of advice from the article.
I explained why each idea helps the bones, using words like because.
I used at least two key words, such as nutrient, repair, or protect.
MID.modelAnswer: First, drink milk and eat calcium-rich food, because calcium is the nutrient that makes bones hard and strong. Second, get some sunlight, because it helps your skin make vitamin D, which helps your body absorb calcium. Third, stay active and be careful during sports, because bones need time and rest to repair themselves if they ever fracture.

keyWords.definition: relating to the bones that make up the skeleton
keyWords.example: The X-ray showed no sign of skeletal damage after the accident.

keyWords.definition: a flexible, rubbery tissue found in joints and in growing bones
keyWords.example: The tip of your nose feels bendy because it is made of cartilage.

keyWords.definition: a natural substance from food or the earth that the body needs, such as calcium
keyWords.example: Iron is a mineral that helps carry oxygen through the blood.

keyWords.definition: to grow back or form again after damage
keyWords.example: Some lizards can regenerate a tail they have lost.

keyWords.definition: to reshape or rebuild something into a better form
keyWords.example: The city plans to remodel the old library building next year.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: Bone is a living tissue that grows through cartilage-based growth plates and can regenerate itself through a structured healing and remodeling process.
Bones are essentially inert structures that never change once puberty ends, and they cannot heal at all after a break or a crack in the arm or leg.
Marrow is the single most important factor in determining skeletal health, and the growth plates play no part in how bones grow.
Fractures permanently weaken a bone, leaving it unable to regain its original strength, so a broken bone never heals as well as before.
questions.why: The article describes cartilage growth plates, mineral deposition, and the staged healing and remodeling that restores a fractured bone.

wrong.B: The article shows bone density can still change in adulthood through mechanical stress.
wrong.C: Marrow is one structure among several discussed, not singled out as most important.
wrong.D: The article explains remodeling restores a structure nearly indistinguishable from the original.

questions.stem: According to the article, where specifically does bone lengthening occur?
options: Throughout the marrow cavity in the center of every bone
At growth plates composed of cartilage near the ends of long bones
Within the compact outer layer only, near the surface of the bone
Inside the protective hematoma that forms after a break in the bone
questions.why: The article states lengthening occurs at growth plates, bands of cartilage near the ends of long bones.

wrong.A: Marrow produces blood cells, not length.
wrong.C: The compact layer provides strength, not lengthening.
wrong.D: The hematoma relates to fracture healing, not normal growth.

questions.stem: Which two minerals does the article identify as being deposited within bone's protein framework?
options: Phosphorus and sodium
Iron and potassium
Calcium and phosphorus
Calcium and iron
questions.why: The article names calcium and phosphorus as the minerals deposited in bone's protein framework.

wrong.B: Iron is not mentioned as a bone mineral in the article.
wrong.D: Iron is not mentioned.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word regenerate most nearly mean?
options: To weaken permanently
To grow back or form again
To absorb completely
To remain exactly unchanged
questions.why: The article uses regenerate to describe the fracture site forming a structure nearly identical to the bone's original form.

wrong.A: Regenerating is the opposite of weakening.
wrong.C: Absorption relates to calcium intake, a different idea.
wrong.D: Regenerating implies change and renewal, not staying the same.

questions.stem: How does the author structure the discussion after introducing the skeleton's basic functions?
options: By narrating one patient's hospital visit from start to finish, with each doctor, each room and each test
By explaining a sequence of related topics: growth, structure, minerals, healing, and mechanical loading
By ranking every bone in the body from strongest to weakest, with a score for each one
By arguing against a commonly held scientific theory, and then showing why it is false
questions.why: The article moves through growth, internal structure, minerals, fracture healing, and the effect of exercise on bone density.

wrong.C: The article does not rank bones by strength.
wrong.D: The article presents accepted explanations, not an argument against a theory.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what effect does prolonged inactivity have on bone?
options: It causes growth plates to reopen.
It converts spongy bone into marrow.
It tends to reduce bone density over time.
It accelerates the remodeling phase after a fracture.
questions.why: The article says bones that remain largely unloaded tend to lose density over time.

wrong.A: Growth plates close permanently after puberty regardless of activity.
wrong.B: Marrow and spongy bone are distinct structures that do not convert into each other.
wrong.D: Remodeling speed is not linked to inactivity in the article.

questions.stem: A teenager who has just finished puberty wants to become several centimeters taller through bone lengthening. What would the article suggest?
options: This is likely, since growth plates stay open for several more years.
This is unlikely, since the growth plates have already closed.
This is possible only if the teenager increases calcium intake dramatically.
This is possible only through intense weight-bearing exercise.
questions.why: The article states growth plates close permanently once puberty concludes, making further lengthening impossible.

wrong.A: The article says growth plates close at this point, not stay open.
wrong.C: Calcium supports bone strength, not lengthening after plates close.
wrong.D: Exercise affects bone density, not length after growth plates close.

questions.stem: How are osteoblasts and osteoclasts different, according to the article?
options: Osteoblasts remove bone, while osteoclasts deposit new bone.
Osteoblasts are found only in marrow, while osteoclasts are found only in cartilage.
Osteoblasts cause fractures, while osteoclasts prevent them.
Osteoblasts deposit new bone, while osteoclasts remove excess or misshapen bone.
questions.why: The article explains that osteoclasts remove excess or misshapen bone while osteoblasts deposit precisely shaped new bone during remodeling.

wrong.B: The article does not restrict either cell type to marrow or cartilage alone.
wrong.C: Neither cell type is described as causing or preventing fractures.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how a bone grows through childhood and how it regenerates itself after a fracture, using specific details from the article.
checklist: I explained the role of cartilage growth plates in bone growth.
I described the stages of fracture healing, including remodeling.
I used at least two key words, such as mineral, skeletal, or regenerate.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Throughout childhood, cartilage at the growth plates gradually converts into bone, lengthening the skeletal frame until puberty ends and the plates close. Minerals such as calcium and phosphorus make this bone rigid and strong. When a fracture occurs, the body forms a clot, builds new bone, and then enters a remodeling phase in which the fracture site can regenerate a shape nearly identical to the original bone.
